newsitem.title: USA: U.S. crop insurer fined $2 million in Espy probe.
newsitem.headline: U.S. crop insurer fined $2 million in Espy probe.

text.p: The second largest crop insurance company in the nation was fined $2 million on Tuesday after entering a "no contest" plea to charges of funnelling illegal campaign contributions to the brother of former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy.

Crop Growers Corp. of Great Falls, Montana, had also been charged with falsifying its books and records in the illegal scheme to help Henry Espy and gain access to his brother who was then a member of the Clinton Cabinet.

The $2 million fine is the largest criminal fine ever imposed in an Indepedent Counsel matter, said an aide to attorney Donald Smaltz, the special prosecutor who is conducting a probe of the former Cabinet secretary which resulted in the charges against Crop Growers.
The former chairman of Crop Growers, John Hemmingson, was convicted last month along with New Orleans attorney Alvarez Ferrouillet of money-laundering illegal compaign contributions to Henry Espy.

Former Agriculture Secretary Espy has been under special investigation by Independent Counsel Smaltz for over two years for illegally accepting gifts and favours while he was head of the huge federal agency, from companies his department was in charge of regulating.

So far, the probe has resulted in criminal indictments and charges being brought against more than a dozen individuals and concerns, including the Washington lobbyist for the nation's biggest chicken processor, Arkansas-based Tyson Foods.
The investigation has also yielded convictions of Sun-Diamond Growers of California, the nation's largest fruit cooperative, in addition to the recent convictions of Hemmingson and Ferrouillet.

Hemmingson and Crop Growers former executive vice president Gary Black were also named as co-defendants in the indictment against the company, but they did not enter pleas on Tuesday. An official said their trial was scheduled to begin later this month.
"We think we can prove the defendants guilty beyond a reasonable doubt," Smaltz told Reuters from his California office.

In the illegal scheme, Crop Growers defrauded the Federal Election Commission by concealing and disguising $46,000 in illegal corporate contributions to the Henry Espy for Congress campaign in 1993 and 1994.

The scheme involved disguising corporate contributions in 1993 totalling $26,000 as individual contributions from various employees, related parties and their spouses, and of making an additional $20,000 corporate contribution in 1994 to Henry Espy's campaign debt retirement effort through New Orleans attorney Ferrouillet.

The illegal contributions were made "so that Crop Growers and its principals could gain access to then Secretary of Agriculture Mike Espy for the purpose of favourably influencing him on issues of interest to Crop Growers," said the announcement from Smaltz's office. If indicted, Espy would be the first Clinton Cabinet member to be formally charged with criminal wrongdoing.
